In my first few years trading, I saved +10,000s of charts into a playbook and studied the greatest traders I could find until the patterns almost became subconscious.

Funny enough, over the last year I’ve barely looked back at those old charts. And it wasn't because they stopped being valuable, but because after +6 years of staring at charts every day, eventually pattern recognition starts becoming second nature.

I don’t think newer traders realize how powerful building a playbook is in the beginning.

You’re basically training your eyes with thousands of reps before real $$ is on the line. At some point you may outgrow needing to study it constantly, but I genuinely think it was one of the best foundations I built early on.

Fascinating looking back at it now… curious if other experienced traders eventually stopped reviewing old charts as much too?

When I'm trying to figure out whether institutions are accumulating a stock, I look for evidence in price + volume.

I'm looking for these 4 footprints:

1) Higher lows = buyers are stepping up.
2) Stage 1 → Stage 2 transition = the character of the stock may be changing.
3) Volume drying up on pullbacks into the 9/21EMA = sellers aren't showing much urgency.
4) Relative strength vs. the market + its peers = capital is flowing somewhere for a reason.

None of these things mean a stock "has" to go higher.

But when I start seeing multiple layers of probability stack up, I start to watch. That's basically my entire process:

Find the footprints + isolate the leaders + wait for tight risk + sit in stage 2 stocks = butter:)

When I first started out, I watched the screen and traded every single second the market was open. There was absolutely zero control. 

I felt like I had to be in everything, all at the same time. I was constantly running from one stock to another just because the new one looked a little better or was moving a little faster. It was pure exhaustion.

After a few years of getting chopped up, everything shifted:

Now, I trade less and watch more. 

I can sit there and see 20 great ideas cross my desk, and I will only execute on 5 of them. 

That is the simple math of a professional trader. 

You do not need more trades to make more money. You need more patience, tighter execution, and the discipline to let good setups pass so you can load the boat on the elite ones.

Risk-to-reward (R:R) tells you how much you could make relative to what you’re risking.

If you risk $100 to potentially make $300, that’s a 3:1 R:R—or a 3R target.

But a high R:R means nothing without a realistic probability of reaching it. Trading expectancy comes from balancing win rate, average winner and average loser—not simply chasing the tightest stop and biggest target.

One of the most intellectually rewarding phases of the market are the “turning points”

These are points that rhyme with the past market conditions I’ve traded and where I can measure my own growth - not just by my P&L, but by how my decisions, reactions, and emotional control compare to prior cycles. These moments tend to put most participants offsides, and that’s exactly why they’re so revealing

If you study your emotions, your actions, and the instincts that flare up during these shifts, you start to recognize patterns.. subtle signals you completely missed in earlier years. Think of it as technical analysis of your own mind. There are patterns. You respond in a certain way in a certain tape

And so with enough cycles, you realize that the real separation between traders isn’t created during strong, obvious trends. Anyone can participate in momentum. The real difference shows up at the inflection points - when the trend is ending, when conditions are dynamic, when uncertainty is highest, and when clarity is nowhere to be found

The beauty of being a longterm student of the markets is that these moments repeat over and over in some shape or form. You begin to recognize echoes of past cycles, almost like familiar emotional fingerprints. And because turning points don’t happen often, each one becomes a yardstick - an honest piece of feedback from the market to you, about how far you’ve come and how much further you can go

There is no end to learning or improvement. You can always get better. You just need the right reasons to drive you.

I was literally lying in bed thinking about this and had to get back up to write it down.

I don’t think most people actually want to be great. They like the idea of being great.

They want to be profitable, build the business, have the freedom, be at the top of whatever industry they chose. Everybody says, “I’m going to lock in,” because saying it feels good. But I’ve watched the same thing happen over and over again. You get a group of guys together and say, “Let’s wake up early. Let’s do this every day. Let’s actually get after it.”

Day 1, everybody’s there.

Day 3, half the room disappeared.

Give it enough time and almost everybody eventually goes away.

That realization genuinely changed how I think about competition. There really aren’t THAT many people willing to show up for the boring work continuously when nobody is watching, and there’s no immediate reward attached to it.

I spent years+ sitting behind a screen flipping through charts for absolutely stupid amounts of time. There were stretches where I’d study for 12-18 hours, go to sleep thinking about markets, wake up thinking about markets, build playbooks, journal losses, study traders better than me, and then do the exact same thing again the next day.

Was that completely delusional? Yeah, probably looking back...

...but I’m increasingly convinced you need a little bit of delusion to become exceptional at anything.

Everyone wants the breakthrough. Very few people want the 900+ boring days that happen before it. Everyone wants to “make it.” Very few people become obsessed with getting 1% better when there’s 0 evidence yet that any of the work is actually going to pay off.

And I’m definitely not even close to the tip of the iceberg. I’m 22 years old and painfully aware of how little I know. But I know one thing about myself... I’ll keep showing up when others don't.

Talent matters, intelligence matters, who you learn from & surround yourself with matters. But eventually, a LOT of people simply stop showing up.

...and that's okay.

Just don't let it be YOU.

Goodnight & God bless.

- iain 🩵
